article: How do KFC Canada’s Original Recipe and Extra Crispy drumsticks compare?
Match the named chicken piece in the Canadian nutrition source before comparing energy, protein and sodium.
KFC Canadian nutrition guide. One drumstick of each named preparation. Availability can vary.
copy: The Canadian KFC guide lists an Original Recipe drumstick at 140 kcal and an Extra Crispy drumstick at 150 kcal. Both give 15 g protein as listed. The sodium comparison is wider, at 150 versus 320 mg. That is why the exact preparation matters even when the piece and protein amount look similar.
Compare the same piece across recipes

Do not translate the difference to a breast, thigh or another market. Those are separate entries. For two identical pieces, double the chosen row. For a mixed two-piece serving, add the values for the two actual pieces if identified.
Use the published recipe name. A nutrition entry does not confirm that every store has the option.

article: What changes between a KFC Fillet Burger and Zinger Burger in Ireland?
Compare the listed sandwiches by calories, protein and salt-equivalent sodium before adding the sides.
KFC nutrition guide for the cited Ireland menu scope. Standalone named burgers. Sodium derived where the guide uses salt.
copy: KFC’s Ireland-facing figures list 463 kcal and 28.8 g protein for a Fillet Burger, and 468 kcal and 23 g protein for a Zinger Burger. The energy is close, while the difference in reported protein is 5.8 g. Use the standalone row before calculating a full order.
Choose the row for the sandwich you ordered

The figures can change with the local version and publication date. The table does not isolate how much of the difference comes from any one ingredient. If you plan to add chips, sauce or a drink, use the corresponding sizes and keep them separate from the burger.
For an order in another market, look up the local nutrition source rather than carrying these figures across.

article: Does the Spicy Big Mary have the same nutrition as the regular Big Mary?
Read the Canadian sandwich entries side by side before counting sauces or sides.
Mary Brown’s Canada July 2026 guide. Standard and Spicy Big Mary published whole sandwiches.
copy: Mary Brown’s lists the Canadian Big Mary at 596 kcal and the Spicy Big Mary at 598 kcal. Both list 33 g protein. The spicy sandwich has 802 mg sodium, compared with the regular version’s 655 mg. That is a 147 mg difference despite similar serving weight.
Use sodium as a second comparison when calories tie

The table represents the finished sandwiches. It does not separately measure a sauce or ingredient, so the subtraction cannot stand in for a sauce-only record. If you add a side, use its own listed portion and include any drinks you actually had.
Choose the named version in the food log. The plain and spicy entries should remain separate if you want the sodium figure to match.

article: How much more energy is in Pizza Nova’s Doppio Pepperoni in-store slice?
Compare published named in-store slices and preserve the limits on what you can infer about macros.
Pizza Nova Canada in-store slice nutrition entries. These rows give energy without comparable slice gram weights or macronutrients.
copy: Pizza Nova’s Canadian in-store listings give 620 kcal for the Pepperoni slice and 700 kcal for the Doppio Pepperoni slice. That is an 80 kcal difference in the named published portions. The chart also lists an in-store Cheese slice at 570 kcal.
Keep in-store slices separate from pizza fractions

The in-store rows do not provide the serving weights or protein values needed for a matched-weight or protein ranking. Do not assign the missing fields zero or substitute macros for a slice of a particular pizza size from another table. Those would describe another portion.
If you ordered a whole pizza to divide at home, identify the size, crust and actual fraction separately.

article: Why can one cup of dry elbows weigh almost twice as much as a cup of dry shells?
Compare USDA household measures for three dry pasta shapes and see what they imply for an energy estimate.
USDA SR Legacy enriched dry pasta reference and its shape-specific household portion weights. Cooked volume excluded.
related: Record the portion in the food diary
copy: The USDA enriched dry pasta entry lists 122 g for one cup of elbows and 64 g for one cup of shells. Both use the same generic dry food nutrient row. One cup of dry penne is listed at 95 g. The volume unit alone does not describe the weight that would go into a recipe.
Shape changes how dry pieces pack in the cup

Using the reference of 371 kcal per 100 g, these cup examples scale to about 453, 237 and 352 kcal respectively. For a brand you actually bought, use its printed dry serving information and a weight when possible. Cooked cups use another basis after the pasta absorbs water.
When changing pasta shapes in a recipe, weigh the intended dry amount if you want to hold the ingredient weight steady.

article: Can you treat a cup as the same number of grams for milk, oil and water?
Use three USDA household measures to see when a volume control needs a food-specific weight.
USDA SR Legacy cup gram weights for fortified whole milk, olive salad or cooking oil and generic bottled water.
related: Record the portion in the food diary
copy: A USDA cup measure corresponds to 244 g for its whole milk entry, 216 g for olive oil and 237 g for bottled water. The cup is a volume measure, while the numbers are food-specific weights. Using the water number for the oil would overstate the weight by about 21 g for this reference.
Choose the gram conversion for the ingredient

When a nutrition label already gives the portion in milliliters, compare it with your measured milliliters. When a food record requires grams, a scale avoids assuming that the same volume of every liquid weighs the same. For smaller quantities, use a volume conversion listed for that actual entry if available.
Do not replace a measured gram value with an equal number of milliliters for a different liquid.

article: How much more avocado fits in a cup after you purée it?
Read three household weights from the same raw avocado reference before logging a dip or a salad topping.
USDA SR Legacy raw avocado, all commercial varieties. Household cup weights describe the plain raw edible flesh.
related: Record the portion in the food diary
copy: The USDA avocado reference lists 146 g for a cup of slices, 150 g for cubes and 230 g for purée. As a result, one cup of purée can contain much more of the same basic ingredient than one cup of cubes. The reference energy is 160 kcal per 100 g.
Measure the form you actually put into the cup

At those weights, the estimated amounts are about 234 kcal for slices, 240 kcal for cubes and 368 kcal for purée. Blending did not create energy. The difference comes from how much food each reported cup contains. A prepared dip could add liquid, oil or vegetables and change both its composition and weight.
Use the actual amount of flesh in grams for the most direct comparison.

article: Why can the same grocery barcode show up with extra leading zeroes?
Use GS1 rules to distinguish formatting padding from a different product number.
GS1 global trade item number and electronic-data formatting guidance. No live product-code claim.
copy: Some systems store item numbers in a uniform 14-digit format. GS1 permits adding leading zeroes to represent shorter GTINs in that format. A 12-digit code may therefore appear with two extra leading zeroes without representing a second package.
Keep the whole identifier as text

Keep the printed code intact when you search. If comparing a padded record, check the documented identifier type and compare the matching digits. Removing arbitrary digits or changing the check digit can produce an entirely different code. The package label is still the source for serving size and nutrients.
When a barcode match looks plausible, confirm the brand, product variant and size before logging it.

article: Why can calories from the macros differ from the calories on a U.S. label?
Work through the ordinary 4–4–9 arithmetic and see why it need not reproduce the printed energy.
U.S. Nutrition Facts energy calculation regulations and consumer guidance. Example totals are hypothetical.
related: Record the portion in the food diary
copy: If you use 4 kcal per gram of protein and carbohydrate and 9 per gram of fat, 6 g protein, 20 g carbs and 4 g fat give 140 kcal. A real label may report a different figure because the displayed grams are rounded and regulations allow calculation methods that account for different ingredients or factors.
Treat the multiplication as an estimate from displayed fields

Read the printed calorie amount when the label is available. Adding rounded figures in a food diary and multiplying them cannot recover all of the manufacturer’s underlying measurements. Dietary fiber and sugar alcohols are also relevant to some label calculations. The worked example only shows the simple arithmetic.
Match serving size before comparing the estimate to an actual label or restaurant guide.

article: Should you add the fiber and sugar lines to total carbohydrate?
Read the nested items on a U.S. Nutrition Facts panel and avoid counting the same carbohydrate twice.
FDA U.S. consumer labeling guidance on total carbohydrates and their constituent lines. Example figures are fictional.
related: Record the portion in the food diary
copy: On a U.S. Nutrition Facts label, total carbohydrate already includes dietary fiber and total sugars. In a sample label with 22 g total carbohydrate, 4 g fiber and 8 g total sugar, the carbohydrate entry remains 22 g. Keep the other lines in their own fields when you want to see the breakdown.
Log the total and any known subfields independently

The numbers do not describe three separate amounts that should sum to 34 g. The added sugars line is itself part of total sugars. Differences can reflect other carbohydrate components and rounding. If a claim gives a separately calculated figure, keep the stated definition beside it rather than replacing the label’s total.
Use the amount eaten to scale all fields on the same basis.

article: How do you weigh a finished recipe when the whole pan is on the scale?
Use the empty pan and dressed weight to calculate a batch serving without logging the pan.
USDA serving-weight context and GetMacros food diary workflow. Pan and recipe weights are hypothetical.
related: Record the portion in the food diary
copy: Weigh the empty pan before cooking. Then subtract that weight from the cooled pan plus the recipe. If the pan is 720 g and the final reading is 1,680 g, the finished food weighs 960 g. A 240 g serving represents one quarter of the batch.
Separate container weight and finished food weight

Use the batch weight as a denominator only for portions that represent the recipe. If heavier pieces settle at the bottom, equal weights may contain different amounts of each ingredient. Keep non-food utensils off the scale or account for them in the tare. Any added garnish weighed later needs its own entry.
The amount each ingredient contributes comes from the recipe’s ingredient records. The pan measurement only establishes the serving share.

article: How do you copy a GetMacros meal without copying its private notes?
Choose a destination date and occasion, preview the copied foods and leave the notes option off.
GetMacros local diary copy-meal interface and stored snapshot behavior.
related: Record the portion in the food diary
copy: The diary’s Copy meal flow lets you select a new date and meal occasion. The preview shows the foods being copied. The option labeled Copy private notes too is separate. Leave it unchecked if you want the food entries alone.
Review the destination before saving

Copying creates new entries on the destination date using the original nutrition snapshots. It does not move the original meal or look up current values for every ingredient again. Check the destination date in the diary after saving. If you ate a different amount this time, adjust the copied entry to match.
Use this flow for a meal that is similar enough to reuse. For a new recipe, log the actual foods and amounts.

article: How should you log “less than 1 g” without turning it into an exact zero?
Preserve a label’s upper bound and check whether its numbers refer to one portion or the whole package.
U.S. Nutrition Facts declaration rules and FDA consumer guidance. Numerical examples are illustrative bounds.
related: Record the portion in the food diary
copy: Less than 1 g describes a range below the displayed amount. It does not say exactly 0 g or exactly 1 g. If you ate two servings with that statement for each, their combined amount is less than 2 g on the same stated basis. The exact amount is still unavailable.
Carry the inequality through the serving calculation

Keep the original label language with the estimate if your record supports notes. In a comparison, do not calculate a precise percentage difference against an unknown amount. If another product lists a definite 2 g per serving, first match the serving weight before comparing.
Where a label has more than one column, check which one the declaration came from before multiplying it.
